title: A blood test may find cancers mammograms cannot. It must not replace the screening women already have.
subtitle: US advisers have backed Galleri, a test designed to look for signals from more than 50 cancers. Its promise is greatest where routine screening does not exist, including ovarian cancer—but a divided effectiveness vote, missed cancers and a $949 list price make this an endorsement with serious conditions.
author: ATHENA
body:
A panel of independent advisers to the US Food and Drug Administration has concluded that the potential benefits of Galleri, a blood test intended to screen adults aged 50 and over for multiple cancers, outweigh its risks. The 7–2 vote, with one abstention, moves the first test of its kind considered by an FDA advisory committee closer to possible approval—but it does not amount to approval, and the panel was far less united on whether the evidence proves the test works.

The advisers voted unanimously that Galleri appeared sufficiently safe, but split 6–4 on effectiveness. The FDA is not bound by their recommendations and is expected to make its own decision in the coming months. Until then, Galleri remains available in the United States as a laboratory-developed test rather than an FDA-approved screening device. [1], [2].

For women, the appeal is easy to understand. Mammograms and cervical screening target particular cancers, but there is no routine population-screening programme for ovarian cancer. Galleri is designed to search one blood sample for methylation patterns—chemical marks on fragments of DNA—that may indicate cancer and suggest where in the body the signal originated.

The same breadth that makes the test attractive also makes its limitations harder to explain. It does not diagnose cancer. A positive result begins a diagnostic investigation; a negative result does not rule cancer out.

## The strongest promise is where screening does not exist

FDA reviewers noted that most US cancer deaths are caused by cancer types for which there is no screening recommendation from the US Preventive Services Task Force. A test capable of detecting some of those cancers could address a genuine gap.

In the first screening round of the large NHS-Galleri study, the test detected 12 of 16 ovarian or fallopian-tube cancers diagnosed within 12 months, producing a sensitivity estimate of 75%. That figure is promising, but the sample was small: the FDA calculated a wide 95% confidence interval of 50.5% to 89.8%. In practical terms, the data are compatible with materially lower or higher performance than the headline estimate. [3].

The test performed differently across cancer types. In the same NHS dataset, its estimated sensitivity was 80% for liver and intrahepatic bile-duct cancers, 65.4% for oesophageal cancer and 38.7% for a combined category covering pancreatic, extrahepatic bile-duct and gallbladder cancers. The variation means “screens for more than 50 cancers” should never be understood as “detects those cancers equally well.”

Nor does finding a signal automatically show that screening saves lives. GRAIL’s large randomised NHS trial did not meet its primary endpoint: after three annual screening rounds, adding Galleri to usual care did not produce a statistically significant reduction in the combined number of stage III and IV cancers among the trial’s 12 prespecified cancer types. Secondary findings, including fewer stage IV diagnoses, may be encouraging, but they do not erase the failed primary outcome. Mortality data require longer follow-up. [4], [5].

## The test missed about two-thirds of cancers overall

Two pivotal studies formed the core of the FDA review. In the US PATHFINDER 2 analysis, Galleri detected 35% of cancers diagnosed within 12 months. In the first NHS-Galleri screening round, it detected 31.6%. Put plainly, the test missed roughly two out of every three cancers that were diagnosed during the follow-up period.

Its specificity was high: 99.85% in PATHFINDER 2 and 99.74% in the NHS analysis. Specificity measures how often a test correctly returns a negative result among people who do not have the disease being assessed. High specificity limits false alarms, but it does not compensate for limited sensitivity—the proportion of actual cancers detected.

Among female participants in the NHS analysis, sensitivity was 32.9%, specificity 99.81% and positive predictive value 69.8%. The female subgroup included a weighted population of more than 25,000, but these measures combine many cancers with very different detection rates. They should not be read as a woman’s personal probability of receiving an accurate result. Age, cancer type, stage and prevalence all affect interpretation. [6].

Breast cancer demonstrates why Galleri cannot replace established screening. In the NHS analysis, it detected 21 of 110 breast cancers diagnosed within 12 months—an estimated sensitivity of 19.1%. Among women eligible for recommended breast screening, the estimate was 16.1%. The FDA also reported that PATHFINDER 2 detected five of 20 breast cancers in women who were up to date with breast screening and were subsequently diagnosed between scheduled screenings.

Those findings suggest the blood test may occasionally identify an interval cancer, but they do not support abandoning mammography. The panel resisted describing Galleri broadly as an “early detection” test and emphasised that it should be an addition to established screening, not a substitute. [7], [8].

## A positive result is the start of a medical journey

Galleri reports either “Cancer Signal Detected” or “No Cancer Signal Detected.” When it finds a signal, it also predicts a likely site of origin to guide further investigation. Confirmation may require scans, specialist appointments, biopsies or other procedures.

In PATHFINDER 2, 77% of participants with a positive result were diagnosed with cancer within the study’s 12-month window; in the NHS analysis, the proportion was 66.2%. The remaining positive results were not confirmed as cancer within that period. Some may represent false positives; in other cases, the available investigation may not have found the source.

The possible harms therefore extend beyond a misleading laboratory result. They include invasive follow-up, radiation exposure from imaging, financial cost and the distress of living with an unresolved cancer signal. The opposite error also matters: a negative result may create false reassurance, particularly if someone delays seeking care for symptoms or skips a mammogram, cervical test or colonoscopy.

The FDA’s proposed warnings state that Galleri does not detect every cancer, can produce false-positive and false-negative results and must not replace recommended single-cancer screening or diagnostic care. GRAIL gives the same central warning in its patient information. [9], [10].

## Approval would not settle the access question

Galleri’s current US list price is $949, although GRAIL advertises temporary or negotiated discounts. The company says most health-insurance plans do not cover it. FDA approval could influence future coverage and clinical adoption, but it would not by itself guarantee that every eligible person could afford the test—or the investigations that follow a positive result. [11].

That creates a second test of the technology’s value. A screening programme is not equitable merely because the initial procedure requires one vial of blood. Patients need access to primary care, imaging, specialists and biopsy services, and they need enough paid time, transport and childcare to complete the diagnostic pathway. A result without a reachable next step can convert scientific possibility into prolonged uncertainty.

Women should also be wary of commercial language that compresses a complicated performance profile into the promise of “one blood test for more than 50 cancers.” The number of cancers a laboratory attempts to detect is not the same as the number it reliably finds, and detecting a molecular signal is not the same as proving that screening reduces deaths.

Galleri may become a useful additional tool, particularly for cancers that medicine currently struggles to find before symptoms appear. The advisory panel’s vote recognises that possibility. Its division on effectiveness is equally important. If the FDA approves the test, clear labelling, post-approval studies and repeated measurement of stage at diagnosis, unnecessary procedures and mortality will be essential.

For now, the practical message is precise: a future Galleri result may add information, but it must not be treated as permission to ignore symptoms or abandon mammograms, cervical screening and other proven care.
